verdict.summary: Registering a classic GitHub OAuth app is self-service: fill in a short form under Developer settings and it works right away. The research found no review, verification or user allowlist for OAuth apps. What you do need to plan for is scope breadth, the token-expiry setting, and rate limits.
verdict.approval_wait: none (no review found for classic OAuth apps)

steps.title: Decide: stay on Composio managed auth, or bring your own OAuth app
steps.detail: Composio offers a managed GitHub OAuth app, so you can start without registering anything. Register your own app when you want your own client ID/secret, your own branding on the consent screen, or tighter scopes. GitHub's docs recommend a GitHub App over an OAuth app for new builds, but this guide covers the classic OAuth app.

steps.title: Sign in and choose who owns the app
steps.detail: Sign in to github.com. Decide whether the app should belong to your personal account or to an organization where you are an admin. An org-owned app is easier to hand over later.
gotchas: Each user or organization can own at most 100 OAuth apps.

steps.title: Open the new OAuth app form
steps.detail: Click your profile picture, then Settings > Developer settings > OAuth apps > New OAuth App. If this is your first app, the button says 'Register a new application'. For an org-owned app, start from the organization's settings instead.

steps.title: Fill in the registration form
steps.detail: Enter an Application name and the full Homepage URL of your product. In Authorization callback URL, paste the exact callback URL shown in your Composio auth config. Application description is optional.

values.label: Redirect URI
values.value: Composio callback URL (see the Composio callout on this page)

values.label: Homepage URL
values.value: Full URL of your app's website

gotchas: You can enter up to 10 callback URLs at registration. Matching rules beyond that were not confirmed, so copy the Composio URL exactly.

steps.title: Decide on 'Expire user access tokens'
steps.detail: This option is on by default. With it on, access tokens last 8 hours and are refreshed with a refresh token that lasts 6 months if unused. Leave it on if your setup handles refresh tokens; untick it if your code needs long-lived tokens.
gotchas: Switching expiry on later only affects new tokens. Existing users must sign in again to get expiring tokens.
Even with expiry off, requesting the offline_access scope on a sign-in returns an expiring token plus a refresh token.

steps.title: Enable device flow only if you need it
steps.detail: If your agent runs headless and will use device flow, tick the device flow option in the app settings. Device flow stays off until you enable it. Device codes expire after 15 minutes by default.
gotchas: Device-flow user code submissions are capped at 50 per hour per app.

steps.title: Copy the client credentials into a Composio custom auth config
steps.detail: Register the app, then copy its Client ID and a client secret from the app's settings page. In Composio, create a GitHub auth config that uses your own OAuth credentials and paste them in. The endpoints are https://github.com/login/oauth/authorize and https://github.com/login/oauth/access_token.
gotchas: GitHub does not publish an OIDC discovery document at github.com/.well-known/openid-configuration, so use the explicit authorize and token URLs.

steps.title: Narrow the scope list
steps.detail: Composio's default list (repo, user, gist, notifications, project, workflow, codespace) is broad. An agent can map the tools you actually use to the smallest set of scopes and update the auth config. Scopes are a space-separated list in the authorization request.
gotchas: repo also covers org projects and team memberships, and workflow allows editing GitHub Actions workflow files. Request them only if you need them.
Scopes never grant more than the signing-in user already has.

steps.title: Run a test authorization with your own account
steps.detail: Start a Composio connection, approve the consent screen, and check that a token comes back and an API call works. The flow is authorization code with PKCE (S256 only). An invalid client_id only shows up after GitHub login, so a working sign-in page does not prove your client_id is valid.
gotchas: The temporary code expires after 10 minutes.

steps.title: Handle reduced scopes and rate limits before rollout
steps.detail: Make sure the app handles users who grant or keep fewer scopes than requested. Avoid repeated sign-ins and token churn: there is a cap of 2,000 token requests per hour per app, and users who sign in more than 10 times in an hour are forced to re-authorize.

steps.title: Open to users (no review step)
steps.detail: Share your connection flow with users. The research found no verification, review or install cap for classic OAuth apps. Only list on GitHub Marketplace if you want discovery; that listing is a separate process and was not researched.

requirements.item: Signed-in GitHub account (personal, or admin of the owning organization)
requirements.detail: Developer settings require login. Org-owned apps need admin access to the org.

requirements.item: Application name, Homepage URL, Authorization callback URL
requirements.detail: The only required form fields. Description and device flow are optional.

requirements.item: Refresh-token handling if token expiry stays on
requirements.detail: Access tokens expire after 8 hours. Each refresh returns a new access token and a new refresh token.
2,000 access-token requests per hour per OAuth app.

scopes.effect: Full access to private repos, plus org projects and team memberships. Users see it on the consent screen. No extra review.
Lets the app edit GitHub Actions workflow files. Drop it unless your agent changes CI.
Includes user:email and user:follow. Use user:email alone if you only need the email address.
Full-management scopes. No review is tied to them, but users may refuse or reduce them later.
Returns an expiring token plus a refresh token for that sign-in, even if app-wide expiry is off. It is not shown as a normal scope on the consent prompt.

blockers.symptom: New tokens can't be issued for a while; connections fail across users
blockers.cause: The app went over the limit of 2,000 access-token requests per hour
blockers.fix: Reuse and refresh stored tokens instead of re-authorizing, and spread out bulk onboarding.

blockers.symptom: A user is suddenly asked to re-authorize the app
blockers.cause: They signed in more than 10 times within an hour
blockers.fix: Cache their connection and stop repeating the sign-in flow.

blockers.symptom: Connections stop working about 8 hours after authorization
blockers.cause: 'Expire user access tokens' was on by default and the token was not refreshed
blockers.fix: Make sure the refresh flow runs, or untick the option before onboarding users. Already-issued tokens are not affected by changing it.

blockers.symptom: You can't create a new OAuth app
blockers.cause: The account or organization already owns 100 OAuth apps
blockers.fix: Delete unused apps or register the new one under a different organization.

blockers.cause: Device flow was never enabled in the app settings, or the 50 submissions/hour cap was hit
blockers.fix: Enable device flow in the app settings and throttle code submissions.

composio.note: You can start on Composio's managed GitHub OAuth app with no setup of your own. Switch to your own OAuth app when you want your own branding on the consent screen, your own client ID/secret, or a narrower scope list. Composio's defaults include repo, workflow and codespace, which is more than most agents need. Registering your own app takes about 15 minutes and needs no review, so switching costs little. Paste the callback URL from your Composio auth config into GitHub's Authorization callback URL field.

open_questions: The research found no review, verification or listing requirement for classic OAuth apps. GitHub Marketplace publisher verification and listing rules were not researched.
Redirect URI matching rules beyond the 10-callback limit (exact match, subpaths, localhost) are not confirmed.
Composio's toolkit output gives /api/v1/auth-apps/add as the default redirect, but a probe saw /api/v3/toolkits/auth/callback. Use whatever your Composio auth config shows.
Whether Composio refreshes GitHub's 8-hour expiring tokens correctly has not been tested end to end.
The exact console labels for generating and copying the client secret were not captured in the findings.
Whether the 100-app cap and rate limits differ for new or unreviewed apps is not stated in the docs.
